traits: Shallow, cone-shaped holes dug overnight, 1-3 inches deep
Armored, cat-sized (15-17 inches, 8-17 lbs), terrible eyesight
Long, tapering snout and large front claws for digging
Digs where soil is soft and grubs or earthworms are plentiful

look_alikes.difference: Armadillo holes are small, cone-shaped, and scattered overnight; feral hog rooting tears up much larger patches of turf and soil in a single visit.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot showing the size and shape of the disturbed area.

safety_line: Florida armadillos can carry the bacteria that causes Hansen's disease (leprosy). Don't handle one bare-handed, and wash your hands after any contact with soil it's dug in.

copy.what_it_means: It's likely digging for grubs and earthworms in soft soil, but digging alone doesn't prove which — armadillos eat both, so removing grubs isn't a reliable way to send it elsewhere. Florida allows a licensed nuisance-wildlife trapper to live-trap and relocate it under FWC rules; don't handle one bare-handed.
copy.fact: When startled it jumps straight up — a reflex that surprises people more than it protects the armadillo.
copy.blurb: Digs overnight for grubs and earthworms in soft soil. A wildlife trapper can live-trap and relocate it under FWC rules — don't handle one bare-handed.

tech_notes: Armadillo digging correlates with grub/earthworm presence, but removing grubs is not a documented reliable deterrent per UF/IFAS. Refer to a licensed nuisance-wildlife trapper; FWC rules allow live-trap and release on-site, in-county relocation, or euthanasia. Advise against bare-hand contact (Hansen's disease association in Florida armadillos).
